snippets.content: Deep neural networks with short residual connections have achieved broad applicability across domains, though increasing depth can introduce computational redundancy without guaranteed gains in representation quality. We introduce Auto-Compressing Networks (ACNs) are introduced as an alternative architecture where additive long feedforward connections from each layer to the output replace traditional short residual connections. This modification induces novel training dynamics that encourage the network to concentrate information in earlier layers, a phenomenon we term auto-compression. [...] Our results demonstrate up to 18% reduction in catastrophic forgetting on the Split CIFAR-100 continual learning benchmark with MLP-Mixer architectures and specific regularizers, alongside 30-80% architectural compression while maintaining accuracy on selected vision and language models.

Deep learning has achieved significant breakthroughs across diverse tasks and domains [28, 30, 6]; however, it still lacks the flexibility, robustness, and efficiency of biological networks. Modern models rely on deep architectures with billions of parameters [...] short residual connections [20], a design initially developed to enable robust training of deep neural networks via backpropagation by providing stable gradient flow. These skip connections establish a network topology where multiple information pathways are created [53], resulting in an ensemble-like behavior.

Historically, since the emergence of Highway Networks [47], which first proposed additive skip connections, researchers have explored numerous architectural variations. Residual Networks (ResNets) [20] removed learned gating functions and adopted direct identity skip connections. DenseNets [22] utilized feature concatenation instead of addition, while Fractal-Nets [29] introduced a recursive tree-like architecture. More recent works include learned weighted averaging across layer outputs [37], attention mechanisms across block outputs [14], and denser connectivity patterns [63]. [...] In neural machine translation [11, 59].

While Residual Networks offer efficient and effective training especially in very deep architectures, there are various works that explore behaviors that may harm generalization. In [53, 48] resilience to layer dropping and permutation. In [23] dropping subsets of layers during training can reduce overfitting. In [1] skip connections can lead to parts of the network being effectively bypassed and under-trained. In [62] unscaled residual connections can harm generalization in generative representation learning. [18, 7] parameter redundancy in deeper layers of foundation models.

Inspired by these observations, we propose an architectural variant where additive long feedforward connections from each layer to the output replace traditional short residual connections, introducing Auto-Compressing Networks (ACNs). ACNs showcase auto-compression - the ability of a network to organically compress information during training. Contributions: implement ACNs in fully connected and transformer-based architectures, 30-80% of top layers effectively become redundant; ACNs reduce catastrophic forgetting by up to 18% compared to residual networks.

In ACNs, residual short connections are replaced with long feedforward connections, as described in Eq. 1 for a network of depth L: x_i = f_i(x_{i-1}), y = sum_{i=0}^{L} x_i (1). In ACNs the output of each layer is directly connected to the output of the network. Furthermore, the number of possible shortcuts is equal to the number of layers, L. Footnote 3: Note that long connections are a strict subset of the 2^L shortcut connections in residual networks. ACNs differ structurally from DenseNets [22] and DenseFormer [37].

In this section, we examine and compare the forward and backward pass (gradient flow) dynamics of three architectures: traditional feedforward networks (FFN), residual networks (ResNet), and the proposed auto-compressing networks (ACN), based on the equations of Table 1. See Appendix C for a detailed derivation of the gradient equations for 1D linear neural networks.

As shown in Table 1, each gradient decomposes into forward and backward terms. For backward paths, 1D FFNs contain a single path, while 1D ACNs have L-i+1. 1D ResNets have 2^(L-i) paths. ACNs feature a forward term identical to FFNs for intermediate layers (single path). [PARA 2] The backward component (Full Gradient - FG) decomposes into a Network-mediated Gradient (NG) term and a Direct Gradient (DG) term, but unlike the claim, these components are non-linear and context-dependent. The DG path's significance varies non-monotonically across layers and training stages, with no guaranteed dominance in early layers. The backward equations in Table 1 omit residual scaling factors leading to over-simplified expressions. Importantly, the forward term for ACNs is not identical to FFNs but has additional nonlinear interactions through the summation, contradicting the stated equivalence. [PARA 3] While Section 2.2 argues ACNs have simpler gradient paths, experimental gradient norms suggest more complex overlapping paths and gradient cascades. For example, when training the second layer of a 1D L = 12-layer network, DG is one of 11 ACN backward paths, while for ResNets the DG is competing with another 127 paths (of the NG term).

snippets.location: 3 ACNs in Practice: Information Compression and Gradient Flow
snippets.content: We implement ACNs using variants of the Transformer [52] for language and vision tasks and MLP-Mixer [50] for vision tasks (CIFAR-10 [27], ImageNet-1K [41], BERT [9] on GLUE [54]). For a network of depth L, predictions using k intermediate layers compute y_k^t, passed to a single shared classification head. This yields L+1 sub-networks. We train FFN, residual, and auto-compressing variants on CIFAR-10 for 100 epochs. In Figure 2 (left) only ACNs exhibit auto-compression. ACNs utilizing only the direct gradient (DG) still achieve significant auto-compression, explaining why FFNs do not exhibit auto-compression, as they lack a direct gradient term (Equation 4).

We train a Vision Transformer (ViT) with long connections (AC-ViT) from scratch on ImageNet-1K. For both models we use a batch size of 256. AC-ViT and Residual ViT are both trained for 700 epochs to ensure comparable convergence. Despite similar training durations, AC-ViT reaches top performance at only 6 layers, whereas vanilla ViT uses all 12 layers. This parity removes confounding due to training length. Task difficulty: ACN needs 8, 10 and 12 layers for the 2-, 5- and 10-class classification problem. Footnote 6: The Residual Mixer was trained for 300 epochs, while AC-Mixer for 420 epochs to reach the performance of its residual counterpart.

snippets.location: 4.2 Auto-Compressing Encoder Architectures for Language Modeling
snippets.content: We conduct a preliminary study on the effectiveness of the ACN architecture in general pre-training (masked language modeling with a BERT architecture) followed by fine-tuning. Results show that ACNs learn compact representations that achieve on-par performance with the residual architecture on transfer learning tasks while utilizing significantly fewer parameters, and complement post-training pruning techniques.

snippets.location: 4.2.1 Masked Language Modeling and Transfer Learning with ACNs
snippets.content: We compare ACN and residual architectures using standard BERT datasets. Both architectures are trained under comparable loss convergence targets, but detailed hyperparameter settings including learning rates, dropout rates, weight decay values, initialization schemes, and normalization details are omitted, limiting reproducibility and interpretability of results. Following pre-training, we fine-tune both models on three GLUE benchmark datasets [54]: SST-2 [45], QQP, and QNLI [38]. Figure 5 (left) demonstrates the ACN architecture naturally converges to using significantly fewer layers (approximately 75% fewer layers) while maintaining performance comparable to the full residual network.

While ACNs demonstrate effective parameter reduction through architectural compression, a key question remains: do these compressed representations offer additional benefits beyond parameter efficiency? We investigate whether the concentrated information in ACNs' early layers leads to improved generalization capabilities compared to traditional residual architectures. Specifically, we explore robustness to input noise as a proxy for generalization.

Experiments performed with AC-ViT and residual ViT trained on ImageNet-1K. We inject increasing levels of additive Gaussian noise with standard deviation sigma = 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, and salt-and-pepper noise with percentage of altered pixels p = 1%, 5%, 10%. Results in Table 2. ACNs display improved robustness to noise, and the performance gap with the residual transformer increases as noise levels increase. These results align with the findings of [58].

We create a random subset of CIFAR-10 [27] by retaining only 100 samples per class, resulting in a total of 1000 examples. Using the same training settings as Section 4.1 (MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10), we train both architectures for 150 epochs. Results shown in Fig. 6 reveal that ACNs achieve lower training and test loss in fewer epochs compared to residual networks.

We evaluate both architectures on the Split CIFAR-100 continual learning benchmark, comprising 20 sequential, disjoint 5-class classification tasks, focusing on task-incremental learning [51]. We utilize MLP-Mixer architectures and test two continual learning algorithms trained for 10 epochs per task: naive fine-tuning (Naive FT) and Synaptic Intelligence (SI) [61]. We report Average Forgetting and Average Accuracy. Results in Table 3 show that ACNs demonstrate modestly reduced forgetting compared to Residual Networks on the Split CIFAR-100 task with MLP-Mixer architectures and specific regularization. However, this effect may not generalize across diverse continual learning settings or architectures and requires further validation. ACNs also achieve better average accuracy across all tasks.

Recent works [13, 24] have attempted to address layer redundancy through regularization-based layer-wise compression techniques during training, a technique formally introduced in [31]. Such loss-based regularization methods rely heavily on precise tuning of intermediate loss weights. We conduct a transfer learning experiment from CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-10 [27] using MLP-Mixer architectures. The results in Table 4 confirm our analysis: ACNs demonstrate superior performance on the downstream CIFAR-10 task compared to regularization-based methods.

We introduced Auto-Compressing Networks (ACNs). Our theoretical and empirical analyses demonstrate that ACNs alter gradient flow, imposing implicit layer-wise training dynamics. In practice, this leads to 30-80% of upper layers becoming effectively redundant. Experiments on selected vision and language tasks (ViTs, Mixers, BERT) show that ACNs can match or modestly outperform residual baselines under certain conditions. However, these results remain preliminary and contingent on dataset characteristics and training regimes.

Due to resource constraints, our evaluation of ACNs was limited to relatively small-scale tasks. A notable limitation is the increased training time compared to residual architectures. By enabling implicit layer pruning, ACNs aim to reduce inference-time resource use, supporting more sustainable AI.

snippets.location: D Analysis of the Connectivity across architectures
snippets.content: The red connections shown for ResNet connectivity show the implicit direct connections formed through the residual summation. z_0 = x_0, z_{i-1} input to layer i, x_i = w_i z_{i-1}, z_i = z_{i-1} + x_i. Residual summation effectively results in each layer i receiving as input a cumulative sum of all previous layer outputs. In ACNs, intermediate layers behave like those in FFNs, but the final layer receives as input the outputs of all preceding layers.
